questions.q: What does IBM's Quantum Volume (QV) benchmark actually test?
options: The largest 'square' random circuit -- using n qubits arranged in n layers of random two-qubit operations -- that a device can run while still matching the ideal output closely enough to pass a statistical threshold
The total number of physical qubits fabricated on the chip, regardless of how they perform
The theoretical maximum qubit count the manufacturing process could someday support
Only the speed in raw clock cycles at which the device executes any circuit
questions.explain: QV is built around finding the largest n for which an n-qubit, n-layer random circuit passes a statistical closeness test against the ideal output -- not a raw hardware spec.

questions.q: If a device's largest passing square circuit has n = 7, what is its reported Quantum Volume, and why does QV use this doubling relationship rather than reporting n directly?
options: QV = 14, because QV is simply n multiplied by 2
QV = 7, reported directly with no transformation applied

QV = 2^7 = 128; the doubling reflects how quickly circuits get harder to run correctly as qubit count and depth grow together, so a modest increase in n represents a much larger real jump in capability
QV = 49, because QV squares the value of n
questions.explain: QV is defined as 2^n specifically because the difficulty of passing the test grows rapidly as n increases, so the exponential score better reflects the real jump in capability between consecutive values of n.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say Quantum Volume is more informative than raw qubit count alone?
options: Because QV's test circuits grow in depth at the same rate they grow in width, so passing at a given n requires enough qubits, enough gate fidelity to survive that many layers, and enough connectivity to avoid excessive SWAP overhead -- forcing all three factors to hold at once
Because QV ignores connectivity and fidelity entirely and measures only raw speed
Because every vendor calculates QV using an identical, universally agreed formula with no circuit testing
Because QV is calculated purely from the chip's physical qubit count with no circuit execution involved
questions.explain: QV effectively forces the 'three-way AND' (qubits, coherent depth, connectivity) into a single pass/fail test repeated at increasing n, so a device can't score well just by having many poorly-connected or low-fidelity qubits.

questions.q: What is a real limitation of Quantum Volume that the lesson identifies?
options: It is mathematically identical to raw qubit count and provides no additional information
It uses one specific random-circuit profile and doesn't directly capture raw execution speed or how a device handles circuits that are much wider than deep or much deeper than wide
It cannot be computed for any real quantum device and exists only as a theoretical construct
It only applies to classical computers, not quantum hardware
questions.explain: QV aggregates information into one number using a specific square-circuit test, so it says nothing about speed (that's what CLOPS measures) and nothing about circuits with very different width-to-depth ratios than the square test circuits use.

questions.q: Why does the lesson caution against trusting any single composite benchmark, including CLOPS or algorithmic qubits, at face value?
options: Because all composite benchmarks are deliberately falsified by every vendor
Because CLOPS and algorithmic qubits measure exactly the same thing as Quantum Volume, making them redundant
Because benchmarks never change over time, so an old number is just as reliable as a current one

Because a benchmark reflects specific test assumptions, and vendors have a natural incentive to promote whichever benchmark happens to make their own architecture look best, so a quoted number should prompt follow-up questions rather than a conclusion
questions.explain: The lesson's core caution is that different vendors emphasize different benchmarks (QV, CLOPS, algorithmic qubits) that favor their own architecture's strengths, and that even QV scores shift as calibration improves -- so any single number is a snapshot and an incomplete picture, not a final verdict.
